title: A contact path for a fintech product
metaTitle: A fintech product contact page that routes
excerpt: Tell a fintech buyer what happens after they reach out, how fast, and what to have ready. The action is to open an account or talk to sales, not to fill ten fields.
alt: A wide city avenue with yellow taxis, tall buildings, and people on the sidewalk, several clear ways through a busy street for a contact path that should offer one clear route.
caption: An avenue, taxis, and people who already know where they are going. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a fintech contact page say?
faqs.answer: Say which path the person is on, what happens after they submit, how soon a person replies, and what to have ready. Opening an account and talking to sales are different paths and should look different. A single form titled "Contact us" makes the buyer guess which door they opened.

faqs.question: How many fields should the form have?
faqs.answer: As few as you need to route the note to the right person. Name, work email, country, and the job in one sentence are enough for a first sales conversation. Ask for documents, volume spreadsheets, and tax identities after a human has replied, or inside the account application where the reason for each field is clear.

faqs.question: Should support and sales share one form?
faqs.answer: No. A customer with a failed payout needs support, and a prospect who might move money needs sales or an account start. Mixing them trains both groups to write vague notes, and it trains your team to miss the urgent one. Label the doors with the jobs.

markdown:
A fintech product contact page should tell a buyer who may trust you with money what happens after they reach out, how fast, and what to have ready. The action is to start an account or talk to sales.

A form with ten fields is a way to lose them. They already decided to raise a hand. The page should make that hand easy to raise, and make the next hour obvious.

## Two paths, named differently

Most money products have at least two doors, and the page should admit that. One door starts an account. The other books a conversation for buyers who do not fit self-serve. A third door, easy to miss and clearly labeled, is for customers who already have a problem with money in motion. That third door is support. It is not a sales opportunity.

Write the doors in the buyer's words. "Open an account." "Talk to sales about a larger setup." "Get help with a payout." Do not merge them into "Contact us" and sort the mess later. Sorting later means a failed payout sits in a queue next to a newsletter signup. That is an operations bug you can prevent with labels.

If only one door is real, publish one door. A decorative choice between "demo," "partnerships," and "general" with the same destination teaches the buyer that the labels are fake. Fake labels are expensive on a financial product, where the rest of the site is asking for trust.

Put the doors at the top of the page, before the address and the social links. A buyer in a hurry will not scroll past a map to find out whether they can talk to a person. The map, if you need one, is for people who already know they are visiting. It is not the path.

## What happens after they send it

The sentence under the button is the product. "A person on the sales desk reads this and replies with a time or a no." "The account application opens and asks for the entity and a government ID." "Support replies in the same thread." Pick the sentence that is true and put it where the thumb is.

Do not say "we'll be in touch" without saying who and about what. A buyer moving company money wants to know the note will not vanish into a brand inbox that nobody owns. Name the role. You do not have to name a private mobile number. You do have to name a responsibility.

Confirmation belongs on the screen, not only in an email that might land in spam. Repeat what they submitted, or at least the path they chose, and the next step. If you send email too, the email should match the screen. A cheerful automated note that contradicts the page ("a specialist will call in five minutes" when the page said one business day) creates the kind of doubt the rest of the site has been trying to avoid.

If the honest next step is a decline, make room for it. Some prospects are out of country, out of risk appetite, or asking for a product you do not sell. A fast no is a respectful contact path. A slow silence is how people tell their peers you are asleep.

## How fast, said in a way you can keep

Publish a response time you already hit on an ordinary week. If sales replies the same business day, say that. If support for failed payouts is faster than sales, say the two clocks separately. A single "we respond quickly" covers neither and binds you to nothing the buyer can test.

Do not promise a number because a competitor published one. Promise the number your staffing supports. Then design the queue so the promise is boring. A shared inbox with an owner, a status, and a rule for what "replied" means. An auto-reply that only says "we received this" can be part of the clock if the page says the human reply comes after it. It cannot be the whole reply if the page implied a person.

Hours belong next to the clock. A buyer in another region should not have to infer your Tuesday. State the timezone. If you do not cover weekends, say so, and say what happens to a failed payout that lands on Saturday if that case is different. Money products often need that distinction. A marketing site that pretends every note is equal will be corrected by the first real incident.

Speed claims are part of the trust surface. The reader should learn enough to act, including when you will not reply. A time you invented to look attentive fails the first week you miss it. Take the sentence down before a customer quotes it back to you.

## What they should have ready

Tell them before the form, in a short list, what makes the conversation useful. For a sales path, that might be the countries, how money moves today, and the failure they want to stop. For an account start, it might be the legal entity name and the person who can sign. For support, it might be the payout reference, not a novel.

The list is not homework meant to filter out serious people. It is a way to keep the form short. If the list is long, you are asking them to assemble a packet. That packet can be a follow-up, after you have said yes to the conversation. The first contact is a fit check.

Say what you do not need yet. "Do not send full account numbers or identity documents in this form." That sentence prevents a buyer from being more helpful than your security note allows. Give them the channel that is appropriate for documents, and only after the relationship exists. A contact form that invites attachments of passports is a design bug.

Match this list to the pricing and services pages. If those pages said you would ask for volume and entities, ask for that, not for a different set of surprises. The path should feel like one conversation continued, not a new interrogation.

## The short form

Four fields are enough for sales. Name. Work email. Country. What you need, in their words. A dropdown of products is useful only when it matches the service names on the site. A dropdown of twenty internal codes is a test. They will choose "other."

Required fields must be marked in text, not by color alone. Errors must say what to fix and must not wipe the rest of the form. The submit button needs a name that matches the path, "Talk to sales" or "Start application," not "Submit." After a success, focus should move to the confirmation so a screen reader hears it.

WCAG 2 organizes this under understandable and operable content: labels, instructions, and errors a person can perceive, plus controls that work without a precise gesture. The W3C overview is clear that the guidelines cover forms and mobile, not only static articles. A contact form that fails those basics will fail the buyers who need it most, including someone trying to reach you about their own money with a keyboard or a small phone.

Do not add a captcha that sits on the action unless you are already being flooded, and never as the first fix for a quiet site. Do not gate the form behind a newsletter checkbox that is quietly preselected. The buyer came about money, not about your list. If you want permission to send product notes, ask later, in a separate sentence, default off.

## Where the path appears

The contact page is not the only door. The homepage, the pricing page, and each service block should use the same verbs and land in the same flows. A buyer who taps "Talk to sales" in the header should not arrive at a department directory. Deep-link the form with the service already chosen when they came from a service block. Hidden fields are fine. Making them reselect the job is not.

Support should be reachable from the footer and from inside the product, in the same words. The marketing page can point to it for people who are lost. It should not be the visually dominant door for a prospect, or your best sales days will be spent on password resets. The inverse matters too. A logged-in customer should not be dumped on a marketing contact form that asks them to introduce the company.

Publish a real fallback for when the form breaks. A named email address is a respectable fallback if a person reads it. A contact page with only a form, and no other way through, strands the buyer on the day the script fails. Put the fallback in text. Do not put it inside an image of a business card.

Hanabi's public projects show the same preference for a short path over a directory. [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is a useful comparison when you are tempted to add one more field "just in case." The work is specific because the decisions were specific. Your form should be too.

## Review the path with a real note

Once a month, submit each door yourself, on a phone, and see what arrives and when. Check the confirmation, the email, and the queue. If the reply is slower than the page says, change the page or change the staffing. Do not leave a false clock up because the design is already shipped.

Read ten real notes. If people are writing novels in the "what do you need" box, the prompt is too vague or the list above the form is missing. If they are asking questions the pricing page should have answered, fix the pricing page. The contact path is not a place to hide gaps in the rest of the site. It is where those gaps become someone's afternoon.

Keep the fields, the promises, and the routing rules in the same doc as the page. When a role changes, the "who replies" line changes the same week. A contact page that names a person who left is a trust problem you can see coming. Role-based language ages better than a private mobile number, and it still tells the buyer a human exists.

After the path is short, the remaining question is what to take off the rest of the site. [What not to put on the site for a fintech product](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-fintech-product) is the cut list: abstract trust language, and everything else that crowds out the product, the people, and this path.
